questions.answer: The basic sine function \(\sin x\) has period \(2\pi\). For \(\sin(kx)\), the period is \(2\pi/|k|\). Here \(k=3\), so the period is \(2\pi/3\). Therefore \(f(x)=\sin(3x)\) has period \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\).

questions.prompt: A function has period \(4\pi\). Find its fundamental angular frequency \(\omega_0\).
questions.answer: The fundamental angular frequency is related to the period by \(\omega_0=2\pi/T\). Here \(T=4\pi\). Therefore \(\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{4\pi}=\frac{1}{2}\). The fundamental angular frequency is \(\frac{1}{2}\).

questions.prompt: Using the convention \(f(x)\sim \frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(a_n\cos nx+b_n\sin nx)\) on \([-\pi,\pi]\), find \(a_0\) for \(f(x)=1\).
questions.answer: For a \(2\pi\)-periodic Fourier series, \(a_0=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(x)\,dx\). Here \(f(x)=1\), so \(a_0=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}1\,dx\). The integral is \(2\pi\), so \(a_0=2\). Therefore the constant term in the series is \(a_0/2=1\), as expected.

questions.prompt: Using the same Fourier convention on \([-\pi,\pi]\), find \(a_2\) for \(f(x)=\cos(2x)\).
questions.answer: The coefficient is \(a_2=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos(2x)\cos(2x)\,dx\). This is \(\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos^2(2x)\,dx\). Over \([-\pi,\pi]\), the average value of \(\cos^2(2x)\) is \(1/2\), so the integral is \(\pi\). Hence \(a_2=1\). Therefore the \(\cos(2x)\) coefficient is \(1\).

questions.prompt: Using the same Fourier convention on \([-\pi,\pi]\), find \(b_3\) for \(f(x)=\sin(3x)\).
questions.answer: The sine coefficient is \(b_3=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin(3x)\sin(3x)\,dx\). This equals \(\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin^2(3x)\,dx\). The average value of \(\sin^2(3x)\) over whole periods is \(1/2\), so the integral over length \(2\pi\) is \(\pi\). Therefore \(b_3=1\).

questions.prompt: For \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([-\pi,\pi]\), explain which Fourier sine coefficients \(b_n\) are zero.
questions.answer: The function \(f(x)=x^2\) is even because \(f(-x)=(-x)^2=x^2=f(x)\). The sine function \(\sin(nx)\) is odd, so the product \(x^2\sin(nx)\) is odd. The integral of an odd function over \([-\pi,\pi]\) is \(0\). Therefore every sine coefficient satisfies \(b_n=0\).

questions.prompt: For \(f(x)=x\) on \([-\pi,\pi]\), explain which Fourier cosine coefficients are zero.
questions.answer: The function \(f(x)=x\) is odd because \(f(-x)=-f(x)\). The function \(\cos(nx)\) is even, so the product \(x\cos(nx)\) is odd. The integral of an odd function over \([-\pi,\pi]\) is \(0\), so every \(a_n\) for \(n\ge 1\) is zero. Also \(a_0=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x\,dx=0\). Therefore all cosine coefficients, including \(a_0\), are zero.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(x)=1\) for \(0<x<\pi\) and \(f(x)=-1\) for \(-\pi<x<0\), extended with period \(2\pi\). Find the sine coefficients \(b_n\).
questions.answer: The function is odd, so only sine coefficients can be nonzero. For an odd function, \(b_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi}f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx\). On \((0,\pi)\), \(f(x)=1\), so \(b_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi}\sin(nx)\,dx\). The integral is \([ -\cos(nx)/n ]_0^{\pi}=\frac{1-(-1)^n}{n}\). Therefore \(b_n=\frac{2(1-(-1)^n)}{n\pi}\), which is \(0\) for even \(n\) and \(\frac{4}{n\pi}\) for odd \(n\).

questions.prompt: Find the half-range cosine series coefficients for \(f(x)=1\) on \(0<x<L\), using \(f(x)\sim \frac{A_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}A_n\cos\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\).
questions.answer: For a half-range cosine series, \(A_0=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L f(x)\,dx\) and \(A_n=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L f(x)\cos\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\,dx\). Since \(f(x)=1\), \(A_0=\frac{2}{L}\int_0^L1\,dx=2\). For \(n\ge 1\), \(A_n=\frac{2}{L}\left[\frac{L}{n\pi}\sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\right]_0^L=0\). Therefore \(A_0=2\) and \(A_n=0\) for all \(n\ge 1\).

questions.prompt: For the square wave with \(f(x)=1\) on \(0<x<\pi\) and \(f(x)=-1\) on \(-\pi<x<0\), a learner says the Fourier series must equal \(1\) at \(x=0\). Explain the error and give the Fourier series value at \(x=0\).
questions.answer: The error is ignoring the convergence rule at a jump discontinuity. A Fourier series converges to the average of the left-hand and right-hand limits at a jump. At \(x=0\), the left-hand limit is \(-1\) and the right-hand limit is \(1\). The Fourier series value is therefore \(\frac{-1+1}{2}=0\). Thus the Fourier series converges to \(0\) at \(x=0\), not to \(1\).
